about.title: About
about.description: A guided breathing app for the desktop and the web. Free and open source under the GNU GPL 3.0: anyone can use it, study it, change it and share it, and versions they share must stay open source too.
about.issues: Report a problem or suggest an idea
about.inspiration: Inspired by the Prana Breath app for Android. That app isn't available on the desktop, so this one was made to fill the gap. It's an independent project, not affiliated with the Android app.
about.claude: Coded with Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant.
about.credits: Music: “Synthwave 421k” by The Cynic Project and “Blackbird in forest” by carlito62, both in the public domain (CC0). Thank you!
about.learnIntro: Slow, guided breathing is a well-studied way to calm down. Research finds small to moderate benefits for stress, anxiety and mood. Some good places to start reading:

guide.phasesIntro: Every exercise is a cycle of up to four phases, repeated. Breathe gently: comfortably full, comfortably empty, never straining.

phaseText.inhale: Breathe in slowly and smoothly, usually through the nose. Let the belly expand first, then the ribs and the chest. Fill up comfortably, not as much as you possibly can.
phaseText.hold: After breathing in, keep the air in. Stay relaxed: don't clench your throat or tense your shoulders. In yoga this is called antara kumbhaka.
phaseText.exhale: Breathe out slowly and steadily, through the nose or softly through slightly parted lips, until your lungs feel comfortably empty. A long, even exhale is what calms you the most.
phaseText.sustain: After breathing out, pause with empty lungs before the next breath in, staying relaxed. In yoga this is called bahya kumbhaka.

guide.phasesTip: If a phase feels too long, don't push through it: duplicate the exercise in Settings → Exercises and shorten it in your copy, or choose a gentler exercise.
guide.ratiosIntro: Breathing patterns are often written as a ratio of inhale : hold : exhale : sustain. 1:0:4:0 means the exhale lasts four times as long as the inhale, with no holds. The same ratio can be breathed faster or slower: inhale 3 s · exhale 12 s and inhale 4 s · exhale 16 s are both 1:0:4:0.

exerciseText.gentle-start: Even breaths in and out, with no holds, at a comfortable pace. A good first exercise, and a good choice whenever slower breathing feels like an effort.
exerciseText.coherent: Breathing in and out for 5 seconds each: about six breaths a minute. This slow, even pace is the most studied in breathing research, linked to a calmer heart rhythm and less stress.
exerciseText.calm-exhale: Six breaths a minute, with the exhale a little longer than the inhale. A longer exhale is calming; this one stays easy, with no holds.
exerciseText.cyclic-sigh: A full inhale, a short second inhale to top up, then a long, slow exhale: the pattern of a natural sigh. Breathe in through the nose both times. In a 2023 study, five minutes a day of it lifted mood more than mindfulness meditation did.
exerciseText.clear-mind: A long exhale and no holds. Breathing out for longer than you breathe in is the simplest way to slow down and settle a busy mind.
exerciseText.power: A hold after the inhale, then an exhale twice as long as the inhale. Its levels work up to the classic 1:4:2 ratio of pranayama, traditionally used to feel more awake and energised.
exerciseText.harmony: Like Power, with a short pause after the exhale as well, so all four phases are used. A steady, balanced rhythm.
exerciseText.square-breathing: Four equal phases, also known as box breathing. Easy to remember and to count, it's often used to steady yourself in a stressful moment.
exerciseText.relax: An exhale twice as long as the inhale, then a long pause with empty lungs. It slows the breath right down, and suits the time before sleep.

exerciseTune.gentle-start: Easier: 3 s each. Slower: 5 s each, which is Coherent Breathing.
exerciseTune.coherent: Easier: 4 s each. Slower: 6 s each (five breaths a minute).
exerciseTune.calm-exhale: Easier: inhale 3 s · exhale 5 s. A longer exhale: inhale 4 s · exhale 8 s.
exerciseTune.cyclic-sigh: Easier: inhale 2 s · inhale 1 s · exhale 4 s. Slower: inhale 3 s · inhale 1 s · exhale 8 s.

guide.customNote: These are the exercises as they come with the app. They stay as they are (you can change their length and music, and the level of the advanced ones); to make a variation, duplicate one in Settings → Exercises.
guide.disclaimer: Breath Compass is a breathing timer for relaxation and general well-being. It is not a medical device: it doesn't diagnose, treat or prevent any condition, and it is no substitute for advice from a doctor. Don't use it to put off seeing one.
guide.safetyRules:
Breathe gently. Never force a breath or a hold.
Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, light-headed, short of breath, tingling, chest pain or anxiety.
Never practise while driving, in water (bath, pool, sea) or anywhere fainting could be dangerous, and never hold your breath under water.
Start with short, easy exercises and build up slowly.
guide.askDoctor: Talk to a doctor before you start, especially before exercises with long holds, if you:
guide.askDoctorList:
are pregnant
have a heart condition or high blood pressure, or have had a stroke
have a lung condition such as asthma or COPD
have epilepsy or have had seizures
have glaucoma or another eye condition, or have recently had surgery
live with panic attacks, PTSD or another mental health condition: breathwork can sometimes bring up strong feelings
guide.emergency: In a medical emergency, call your local emergency number.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.lead: Breath Compass doesn't collect or send any data. There's no account, no server, no analytics and no tracking: nothing you do in the app leaves your device.

stored.exercises: Your exercises and settings: preparation time, language and phase bells.
stored.sessions: Your session history, for Statistics: for each session of at least a minute, when it started and ended, the exercise, and how long you breathed.
stored.device: This device's preferences: volume and mute, sound levels, theme, session view and colors, the desktop app options, and a random name for this device that keeps its session history in a file of its own.

privacy.whereDesktop: All of it is kept as plain files on this computer: in the data folder below, and the device preferences in the app's own config folder. You can open, copy or delete them at any time.
privacy.whereWeb: All of it is kept in this browser's storage, on this device only. Clearing the browser's data for this site erases it.
privacy.syncDesktop: If you choose a synced data folder, your sync tool (Syncthing, Nextcloud, Dropbox…) copies those files between your devices, under its own terms. The app itself only connects to the internet to check for updates (see Settings → About), and sends nothing about you.
privacy.hostWeb: The web version runs entirely in your browser. The server that hosts it only delivers the page, like any website, and may log that visit; the app sends it nothing.
privacy.links: Links, such as the sources in the Guide, open in your browser only when you click them.
privacy.noCloud: Online accounts and cloud sync aren't planned: there's no server behind this app, and there won't be one. To use it on several devices, sync the data folder with a tool you choose, such as Syncthing, Nextcloud, Dropbox or a folder on your NAS, and pick that folder on each device (see Data folder below).
privacy.noCloudWeb: Online accounts and cloud sync aren't planned: there's no server behind this app, and there won't be one. The web version keeps its data in this browser and can't sync. To use several devices, use the desktop app with a folder synced by a tool you choose, such as Syncthing or Nextcloud.
privacy.backup: To back up your data, copy the data folder. To move to a new computer, copy the folder there and choose it under Data folder.
privacy.backupWeb: There's no backup in the web version: clearing this browser's data, or using another browser, starts from scratch.
privacy.source: The source code is public, so anyone can check what the app does.
